entries.title: feat(accounts): recover the OAuth client pair from the installed core
entries.body:
Token refresh needs an OAuth client id/secret pair that Gravityless does not
redistribute. When data/oauth_client.json was missing, LoadOAuthClient returned
empty strings, the refresh request went to Google without credentials, and every
account ended up with FailedRefreshAttempts = 3 and an apparently revoked token.
The underlying refresh tokens were still valid.

OAuthClientExtractor scans the installed Antigravity binaries for client ids and
secrets, then certifies each candidate pair by attempting a real refresh. The
language server embeds three of each, so position in the binary is not usable as
a discriminator; the live refresh is the only reliable test. Scanning is chunked
so the 174 MB binary is never loaded whole, and a 256-byte carry keeps a pattern
that straddles a chunk boundary.

EnsureOAuthClientAsync caches the resolved pair in data/oauth_client.json, and
RefreshTokenAsync calls it before the first attempt. When no refresh token is
available to verify against, the first candidate is cached unverified so a later
refresh has something to try; a wrong pair then fails visibly instead of being
mistaken for revoked credentials.

Verified against a real core and a live refresh token: nine candidates are found
in 2.5 s, the correct pair is chosen, the cache is written, and the second call
returns from cache in 4 ms.

entries.title: refactor(accounts): populate the OAuth client cache ahead of time
entries.body:
The previous change recovered the OAuth client pair lazily inside
RefreshTokenAsync. That put a 2 s binary scan on the path the user triggers by
clicking refresh, and made the button feel broken.

Extraction now happens where it costs nothing:

  - MainWindow.WarmUpOAuthClient runs once per launch, in the background, and
    returns immediately when the cache already exists.
  - AccountPoolService kicks a fire-and-forget extraction after a successful
    capture. The refresh token captured at that moment is guaranteed live, which
    makes it the most reliable point to certify a candidate pair.

RefreshTokenAsync only reads the cached file. A missing cache now reports that
the core must be synced instead of scanning binaries mid-refresh.

The account pool itself is unchanged: it keeps the refresh token as the durable
credential and treats the stored access token as the most recent known value for
quota display, not as proof of validity. Antigravity renews the access token on
its own once an instance starts.

Verified: warm-up writes the cache in 2.7 s in the background, a subsequent
read takes 7 ms, and a real refresh succeeds against the live account with
FailedRefreshAttempts reset to zero.

entries.title: feat(proxy): report connectivity as a labelled table
entries.body:
The connectivity test collapsed status, latency and reason into one dense text
line, so a failure that never connected was indistinguishable from a slow reply
and long reasons were unreadable.

ProxyTestResult gains GeminiLatencyMeasured and AntigravityLatencyMeasured. A
probe that times out leaves them false, which is how the view separates a
blocked route from a slow one; latency alone cannot, because a failure can still
carry a meaningful elapsed time.

The proxy page now renders a three-row grid: region spanning the value columns,
then one row per probe with status glyph, latency and reason. Status reads ✓, ×
or -; latency reads "<n> ms" or N/A when nothing was measured; the reason is
only filled for failures and skips, and is left-aligned with wrapping because
messages run long.

Batch token refresh now retries transient faults instead of marking an account
dead on first failure, and reports progress through the status strip so a run
over several accounts is not a silent wait.

Verified against a live direct connection from a blocked region: the region row
and both probe rows fill as expected, and the timed-out Gemini probe shows ×
with N/A rather than its 6 s elapsed time.

entries.title: refactor(proxy): label the sampled account by alias, not full address
entries.body:
The connectivity report printed the sampled account's full email in three
places, which is more identifying than the report needs.

ProxyTestResult gains TestedAccountAlias, resolved from the account display
name with the local part of the address as fallback. The alias appears in the
Antigravity row of the report and prefixes a failure reason there; it is also
used inside the probe messages that previously embedded the address.

It is shown even when the probe succeeds, so the row identifies who was tested
rather than only explaining a failure.

Verified that the alias resolves for a display name, an empty name, a malformed
address, and a padded name; the assignment sits after the Gemini gate, so a run
that never reaches the Antigravity probe leaves it null as intended.

entries.title: fix(instances): keep project-less chats out of project storage
entries.body:
A chat started outside any workspace is written by Antigravity with
project_id "outside-of-project" and an empty workspace_uris list. Harvesting
treated such a row as unmatched and fell through to
Projects.FirstOrDefault(), so the conversation was adopted by whichever project
the instance happened to be bound to: its brain moved into that project's memory
directory and the chat appeared under an unrelated name.

ProjectService now recognises both spellings of the project-less id and exposes
IsProjectlessConversation, which also treats an empty id or an empty workspace
list as project-less. ReconcileAndHarvestProjects and SyncMultiProjectOutput skip
those chats instead of relocating them.

The arbitrary FirstOrDefault() fallback is gone. Only the instance's own
"<name>-workspace" project is used when nothing matched; otherwise one is
created, so an unattributable chat can no longer land in an existing project.

Verified IsProjectlessConversation across six combinations: both id spellings,
an empty id, an empty workspace list, and two rows with a real project.

entries.title: fix(instances): verify databases before discarding a copy, and checkpoint on exit
entries.body:
Harvesting decided whether the shared copy was usable with File.Exists alone.
A process killed before checkpointing leaves the .db present but empty, with all
committed pages still in -wal; the harvest then deleted the instance-side copy as
a duplicate and hard-linked the shell, losing the conversation.

IsUsableSqlite checks the file size and the "SQLite format 3" header, and the
harvest now treats an unusable target as absent: the instance copy is promoted
to shared instead of being discarded.

CheckpointInstanceDatabases runs on instance exit, after the process tree is
gone. It issues PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) for every database that still
carries a -wal, so a killed session leaves a merged file rather than an empty
one. Databases without a WAL are skipped to avoid creating and dropping one.

Verified IsUsableSqlite against six states: missing, zero-length, too small, all
zeros, wrong header, and a valid header. Verified the checkpoint against a WAL
database: the -wal is merged and removed, and every row survives.

entries.title: feat(projects): add a memory repair pass for lost conversations
entries.body:
A conversation needs three things to open: a summary row, a checkpoint database
under conversations/, and its brain directory. When the checkpoint database is
lost the conversation can never be opened again, because LangGraph state cannot
be reconstructed from a transcript. Until now nothing reported or salvaged
anything.

ProjectMemoryRepairService.Scan reports every conversation whose checkpoint
database is missing and, separately, every brain directory that has no summary
row at all. Repair re-registers the latter so those conversations return to the
project list, and exports every recoverable transcript to conversation-export.md
beside its brain directory.

The scan opens the summary database read-write: a database whose pages still sit
in -wal refuses a read-only open, which would report an intact project as having
no index. This is the same trap that made the earlier harvest discard good data.

The export renders each step as Markdown and derives the title from the first
user request envelope, falling back to the raw first line.

Verified against the real data root: eleven conversations are reported, two of
them with brain content, and repair exports both, producing a 2.5 MB file for
the 2395-step conversation and a 774-byte one for the 2-step chat.

entries.title: fix(build): fall back through timestamp servers when signing
entries.body:
Signing failed with "The specified timestamp server either could not be reached
or returned an invalid response". The timestamp host was hard-coded to
timestamp.digicert.com in both build.ps1 and sign.ps1, so a single unavailable
host broke every release, and the failure surfaced as a signing error rather
than a timestamping one.

Both scripts now try a list of public timestamp services in order: DigiCert,
Sectigo, Certum, GlobalSign. If none responds the file is signed without a
timestamp, which is a warning rather than an error: the signature is still valid
today and only stops verifying once the certificate expires in 2036.

build.ps1 gained Invoke-SignFile so its two signing sites share one code path
instead of repeating the signtool invocation.

Observed live during this change: DigiCert answered for one installer and failed
for the next executable minutes later, confirming the failure is transient
outage rather than a bad URL. Both files ended up validly signed, the second via
the Sectigo fallback.

entries.title: feat(update): check for app updates from a static manifest
entries.body:
Adds a self-update path independent of the core installer, plus the build-time
version scheme the manifest compares against.

Build version
  Directory.Build.props derives the version from the build date and two local
  counters, matching the release tags:

      yyMM + major + minor   version code   261102
      yy.MM.major.minor      display        26.11.0.2

  Counters come from an optional, gitignored version.props so a release can pin
  them without touching the tracked file. The code is emitted as assembly
  metadata; only the display version is neutralised in Debug builds, so a local
  run can still check for updates.

  DateTime.ToString("yyMM") cannot be used in an MSBuild property function: a bare
  quote ends the expression, and escaping it as %22 makes the format literal. The
  date components are read numerically and padded instead.

Client
  AppVersion parses, normalises and compares version codes. Comparison is numeric
  because ordinal string ordering only matches while every code has the same
  width, and breaks silently the first time a component gains a digit.

  AppUpdateService fetches the manifest and classifies failures instead of
  collapsing them into "network error": a missing or malformed document is the
  publisher's fault, and telling the user to check their connection would send
  them looking in the wrong place.

  AppUpdateInstaller verifies the SHA-512 before launching. A mismatched
  installer is deleted rather than offered, since a corrupted or substituted
  binary has no safe interpretation. Inno Setup is started with
  /CLOSEAPPLICATIONS so it closes this process itself; shutting down first would
  let the installer race the exit.

Server
  The workflow regenerates an orphan info branch on each published release:
  update.json, one changelog per tag in a doubly linked chain, and a
  changelog-index.json fallback if a link is ever broken. Release assets are
  confirmed before the manifest is published, because a manifest pointing at a
  missing asset is the failure that silently breaks every client.

UI
  The Overview app-update card replaces its "coming soon" placeholder with a real
  check, reported through an InfoBar so the status and its progress share one
  surface.

Also converts the remaining inline isEn ternaries in AccountDetailsDialog to
locale keys, and gives PageStatusStrip a themed border so its message does not
read as loose copy on the page background.

entries.title: fix(update): align the manifest with the agreed release contract
entries.body:
Corrects the update manifest before any release depends on it. Nothing has been
published yet, so the schema changes rather than gains a compatibility layer.

Manifest
  The display field is `version`, carrying the dotted form (26.11.0.2), matching
  the release tag's digits. `version_code` stays internal and exists only for the
  comparison. Every property now carries an explicit JSON name, so renaming a C#
  member can no longer silently break the wire format.

  The tag is split at fixed offsets — 2-digit year, 2-digit month, then the major
  and minor counters — because the release process guarantees that width.

Hash removed
  The installer is code-signed, and Windows validates that signature before
  running it elevated, which covers substitution and corruption. A separate
  SHA-512 added a manual publishing step without covering anything the signature
  misses, so it is gone from the manifest, the client and the workflow.

  A truncated transfer is still caught: the download compares the received byte
  count against the advertised size, which surfaces as a clear "incomplete
  download" instead of a generic corruption error at launch.

Index removed
  `changelog-index.json` existed as a fallback for a broken chain. Every run
  rebuilds the whole chain and force-pushes the branch, so a missed or repeated
  run leaves no damage and the fallback has nothing to guard against.

Assets query
  The manifest builder called `gh release view` six times, once per field per
  architecture. It now reads the asset list once and derives both the name and the
  size from that response, so the manifest cannot describe a file that changed
  between calls. Suffix matching replaces substring matching, which would have
  matched the architecture token anywhere in the filename.

OVERRIDE

entries.title: fix(update): route InfoBar text through Message and restore the download link
entries.body:
Both update bars wrote their status into a TextBlock inside InfoBar.Content, but
the WPF-UI template renders only the Message property, so a check reported just a
severity icon with no explanation. The success path of the core check also threw
on display: its locale template still carried a third placeholder for a download
URL that the code no longer supplied, and the FormatException surfaced as a
generic failure.

  - SetUpdateStatus, SetUpdateStage and SetAppUpdateStatus now set InfoBar.Message
    alongside the severity, so every result carries its detail.
  - The direct download link returns as a clickable Hyperlink on its own line in
    the core update bar: the URL is worth showing when the in-app download is
    blocked or slow. It is hidden on every non-success path, since a stale link
    next to an error would offer a file the manifest no longer describes.
  - The CloudUpdate_FoundFormat templates drop the URL placeholder they no longer
    receive, matching the two-argument call.
  - Content now holds only extras (link, progress row); message TextBlocks are
    gone along with their code references.
